title: Mathematicians Hate AI. They Can’t Quit It
gist: NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster accuses OpenAI of using his work to beat him to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem with tens of thousands of agents, yet he and peers like Andreas Thom keep using Codex and ChatGPT because the efficiency gain makes abstention career-threatening. The piece documents attribution collapse in AI-assisted research, OpenAI amending two announcements after mathematicians pushed back, and organized resistance — 25 Fields medalists, 4,000+ Leiden Declaration signatories, 2,000+ Caltech-linked objectors — that participants themselves think is unsustainable.

insights.claim: Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster believes OpenAI used his work to rush ahead and beat him to solving the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, a legendary math problem carrying a $1 million bounty.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: The first high-profile priority dispute between an academic and an AI lab sets the template for IP and credit conflicts as labs target research milestones.
insights.quote: Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster believes OpenAI used his work to rush ahead and beat him to solving a legendary math problem with a $1 million bounty.

insights.claim: Buckmaster says OpenAI deployed tens of thousands of agents to reach the Navier-Stokes solution, but only after it learned the equation was close to being solved.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Massive agent parallelism aimed at problems already near solution is a cheap way to manufacture capability headlines — discount such milestones accordingly.
insights.quote: OpenAI deployed tens of thousands of agents to reach the solution, but only after it learned the equation was close to being solved
insights.locator: Buckmaster had used Codex as well as Anthropic’s competing Claude

insights.claim: OpenAI ran an investigation and amended its Navier-Stokes announcement to state that Buckmaster's Codex prompts over the two preceding months could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Labs are now issuing forensic denials about training-data contamination, a new disclosure category that will invite auditing demands.

insights.claim: German mathematician Andreas Thom says OpenAI's August claim that its Astra model proved a long-standing geometric group theory problem overlooked his 2019 paper and other mathematicians' work, and the company amended its press release after he emailed researchers Mark Sellke and Sébastien Bubeck.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: A second amended announcement in two months suggests systematic overstatement of novelty in AI lab research claims.
insights.locator: So he says he asked OpenAI researchers Mark Sellke

insights.claim: Andreas Thom says he does not trust OpenAI's statement that Buckmaster's prompts could not have influenced the system and concedes he will probably never know whether his own work fed the result.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Unverifiable training-provenance claims mean trust, not evidence, is the binding constraint on lab-academia cooperation.
insights.quote: AI really kills this entire idea that you could trace back who contributed what
insights.locator: While Thom has seen OpenAI’s statement

insights.claim: Humans still do not fully understand each step OpenAI's agents took to arrive at the Navier-Stokes result, which the article frames as an existential problem for a field built on peer review and traceable credit.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: If verification lags generation, the bottleneck in AI-driven science shifts from producing results to certifying them — a market for proof-checking infrastructure.
insights.locator: It’s a big change from how science is typically done

themes.theme: Grievance without exit: usage keeps rising

insights.claim: Despite accusing OpenAI of copying his approach, Buckmaster has continued using the company's coding agent Codex to tidy up his research papers and to reconstruct the logical steps OpenAI's agents may have taken.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Public grievance is not translating into churn, which is the strongest evidence yet that frontier model usage is inelastic to reputational attacks.
insights.quote: Even if you don't agree with any of this, you're kind of stuck. With AI being so useful, it's hard to completely prevent oneself from using it
insights.locator: In the week and half since the New York University professor

insights.claim: Buckmaster characterizes frontier AI providers as holding a monopoly with little choice available to researchers who object to their practices.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Perceived lack of substitutes among sophisticated technical users supports pricing power for the leading labs in research and coding workloads.
insights.quote: These companies have a monopoly, and there is not much choice
insights.locator: “Even if you don't agree with any of this

insights.claim: Andreas Thom continues to use ChatGPT with updated privacy settings to stop his work being used for training because it is extremely efficient at speeding up paper writing, even though he says he would be very angry if a human had used his work without attribution.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Privacy toggles, not abstention, are how technical users reconcile objections with dependence — making enterprise no-train defaults a retention feature.
insights.locator: Thom accepts that his area of study is changing

insights.claim: OpenAI's offerings through universities and at the enterprise level default to not training models on users' data, a contractual distinction that separates academic exposure from consumer-tier exposure.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Data-handling defaults are becoming the sales wedge for institutional AI contracts in research-heavy sectors.
insights.locator: (OpenAI’s offerings through universities

insights.claim: Since August, Cornell mathematician Alex Townsend has seen many colleagues start asking what they need to know about AI and how to set up subscriptions to access higher-powered models.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Academic seat demand for premium model tiers is expanding off the back of the very controversy that was supposed to deter it.
insights.locator: Since August, Townsend has seen many of his colleagues

insights.claim: Andreas Thom argues that attempts to slow AI adoption in mathematics are not sustainable because of the efficiency gain, and that researchers, especially early-career ones, risk being isolated if they do not use AI to accelerate their work.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Competitive isolation risk is the mechanism that converts optional AI tooling into a professional requirement — the same dynamic to expect in law, medicine and finance.
insights.quote: I don't think this is really sustainable because of the efficiency gain
insights.locator: But any attempts to slow things down may be for naught

insights.claim: Twenty-five Fields medalists wrote in an open letter that AI companies and mathematicians are severely misaligned, and more than 4,000 people have signed the Leiden Declaration setting out recommendations for mathematicians, funders and politicians.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Elite scientific bodies mobilizing as an interest group is the precursor to funder mandates and journal policies that could constrain lab research practices.
insights.quote: Twenty-five Fields medalists wrote in an open letter that AI companies and mathematicians are “severely misaligned.”
insights.locator: Some mathematicians are less forgiving

insights.claim: More than 2,000 people with ties to Caltech called on organizers to suspend an AI math hackathon sponsored by Anthropic and OpenAI, and OpenAI has since dropped out of the event.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Campus-level pressure is already forcing labs to withdraw from academic events, raising the cost of university-channel marketing for frontier labs.
insights.locator: That includes more than 2,000 people with ties to Caltech

insights.claim: Buckmaster is calling for a detente in AI-driven mathematics while mathematicians and AI laboratories set ground rules on how to release results, including getting references right.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Expect negotiated publication norms between labs and academic fields to emerge as the practical governance layer, ahead of any regulation.
insights.locator: Buckmaster is calling for a detente

insights.claim: Buckmaster says he will clean up papers he published prematurely to beat OpenAI's announcement, describing one of them as AI slop, an admission that the race dynamic degraded his own output quality.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Competitive pressure from AI labs is measurably lowering the quality bar of human publications, a second-order cost to scientific reliability.
insights.quote: one of which he described as “AI slop.”
insights.locator: He himself is going to clean up the papers

insights.claim: Buckmaster says churning out solutions to long-standing math problems without fully crediting the underlying human work, especially ahead of major IPOs, is irresponsible and childish.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Ties research-milestone announcements directly to pre-IPO narrative building — treat such claims as marketing events with a timing signal attached.
insights.quote: especially ahead of major IPOs—is irresponsible and “childish,”
insights.locator: Showing that AI was pushing the boundaries of mathematics

insights.claim: Buckmaster says showing that AI was pushing the boundaries of mathematics was more important than the result itself, conceding the capability demonstration carries the real value.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Even critics concede capability demonstrations are the product, which is why labs will keep spending compute on headline problems regardless of credit disputes.
insights.locator: Showing that AI was pushing the boundaries of mathematics

insights.claim: Buckmaster warns that using AI merely to clean up grammar could result in years of work being gobbled up in user data and sold to another mathematician or graduate student, which he says is what most mathematicians are worrying about.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Fear of research leakage via routine tool use is the demand driver for on-premise, no-retention and open-weight alternatives in academia.
insights.quote: clean up some of your grammar, and suddenly your years of work [could be] gobbled up in user data and sold to another mathematician or grad student
insights.locator: Buckmaster fears the possibility of using AI

insights.claim: Cornell mathematician Alex Townsend, coauthor of a forthcoming book on the field's evolution, says he feels both excited and nervous, questioning what his purpose is when trillion-dollar companies are in on the game.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Purpose anxiety among mid-career researchers is a leading indicator of talent flows out of academia and into labs.
insights.quote: If I want to make a contribution to mathematics, how do I do that as just a human nowadays when these trillion-dollar companies are in on the game?
insights.locator: Beyond upending attribution

insights.claim: Buckmaster worked on Navier-Stokes using both OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's competing Claude alongside Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge, showing multi-lab tool use and lab-affiliated collaborators inside the same disputed research effort.
insights.speaker: Isabella Ward
insights.so_what: Researchers mixing rival frontier models in one project means tool preference is weakly held and switching costs in research workflows are low.
insights.locator: Buckmaster had used Codex as well as Anthropic’s competing Claude
